opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I was pretty uncertain on both fronts. When I was finishing my undergrad, I had this vague sense that AI safety was important, but I didn't have a strong inside view on whether the technical research people were doing was actually going to matter, and I definitely didn't know whether I'd be any good at it or enjoy it.

The framing that really helped me was to stop treating it as a big, permanent life decision and start treating it as an experiment. The question isn't "Is this my career forever?" It's "What's a cheap way to get information about whether this is a good fit?" I did a few short research stints, internships basically, at different places. Each was a few months, low commitment, and the explicit goal was partly to do useful work and partly just to learn about myself.

The thing I'd really emphasize is that you learn way more from actually trying something than from sitting around thinking about whether you'd like it. I spent a lot of time agonizing in the abstract, and it was pretty unproductive. Then I actually did some research, and within a few months I had much clearer signals. Did I find myself thinking about the problems in the shower? Did I make progress? Did people whose judgment I trusted think the work was promising?

On whether it was useful, I think you have to accept that you're never going to resolve that uncertainty fully up front. The field is young and pre-paradigmatic, and reasonable people disagree a lot about which agendas matter. So rather than waiting until I was confident, I tried to form a rough view, pick something that seemed plausibly valuable, and keep updating as I learned more. Honestly, a lot of my conviction about mechanistic interpretability came after I'd been doing it for a while, not before.

So my general advice is: lower the stakes of the decision, find cheap tests, and pay attention to the evidence you get rather than your prior anxieties. And be willing to walk away if the evidence says it's not for you. That's a perfectly good outcome of an experiment too.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I didn't really know, and I was pretty uncertain for a long time. I'd been interested in AI safety since I was at university, I'd read a bunch about it, I thought it was plausibly the most important problem in the world. But there's a big gap between "this seems important" and "I, specifically, should spend my career on this and would actually be good at it."

And I think the thing that helped most was just trying it. I did an internship, I spent a few months doing research, and I treated it as an experiment rather than a commitment. Because I think people often get stuck in this mode of trying to reason from first principles about whether they'd enjoy research or be good at it, and that's really hard to do from the outside. You can read papers, you can talk to people, but you don't actually get much signal until you sit down and try to do the thing.

The other thing I'd say is that I was pretty worried about the "is this useful" question, like whether the research I'd be doing actually mattered for safety, or whether I'd just be doing something that looked like safety work. And I think I got partly lucky there, in that I ended up in interpretability, which is an area where I could see a clear story for why understanding what's going on inside models would matter, and also where the feedback loops were fast enough that I could tell whether I was making progress. If you're working on something where you can't tell if you're making progress for two years, that's a much harder position to be in when you're uncertain.

But I'd also push back a bit on the framing of needing to be sure. I don't think anyone is sure. The people who seem most confident are often just not thinking about it very hard. I think the right move is to figure out what the cheapest experiment is that gives you real information, do that, and then update. And be willing to leave if it's not working, which is something I think people underrate. The cost of trying something for six months and deciding it's not for you is pretty low, and the information you get is really valuable.

astra-6.text:
I think the key was treating it as an experiment rather than a commitment. There were two separate uncertainties: is technical AI safety research actually useful, and am I someone who can do useful work on it? I didn’t need to resolve both of those before trying anything.

You can spend a long time thinking about whether you’d enjoy research, but actually working on a concrete problem gives you a different kind of evidence. Can you make progress? Do you find the confusing bits interesting? When something doesn’t work, do you want to understand why? And can you get feedback from someone with more experience, rather than judging everything by how productive you feel?

So my approach would be to make the initial decision fairly small: spend some bounded amount of time trying to do research, then reassess. That doesn’t establish that the whole research agenda is valuable—you still need to think critically about how the work could help. But uncertainty about whether something is right for you is often a reason to run an experiment, rather than a reason to wait until you’re certain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key move was realising that I didn’t need to be confident it was useful, or that I was going to be good at it, to justify trying it. Those are quite different bars. If there’s a reasonable chance that this is a really important problem, and a reasonable chance that I could contribute, then spending a few months finding out can be a very good decision.

And trying it gives you information that’s quite hard to get by sitting around thinking. Do I enjoy the actual day-to-day work? Can I make progress on an open-ended problem? When I get stuck, am I curious enough to keep going? Those seemed much more useful questions than “Am I the kind of person who should be an AI safety researcher?”

So I’d frame it as an experiment: pick something concrete, try to get useful feedback, and give yourself permission to discover that it isn’t a fit. You’re making a decision about what to try next, rather than committing the rest of your life.
